back: Many concurrent requests miss the same expired key and all rebuild it from the database at once.

front: How many requests miss during a rebuild?
Why is a stampede a feedback loop?
back: Duplicate queries slow the database, which lengthens the rebuild, which lets even more requests miss.
SET lock:key token NX PX 5000. Winner rebuilds; losers sleep and re-read. Release only if the token matches.
Concurrent requests for the same key in one process share a single in-flight fetch (e.g. Go singleflight, NGINX proxy_cache_lock).
Refresh when now − delta·beta·ln(rand) ≥ expiry: rare far from expiry, near-certain just before it. No locks.
After a soft expiry, one caller rebuilds while others keep getting the old value until the hard TTL.
Requests for keys that exist in neither cache nor database, so every one hits the database.
Caches 'not found' with a short TTL. Stops repeats of the same missing ID; useless against never-repeated random IDs.
No false negatives; tunable false positives. 'Definitely absent' can be trusted, 'possibly present' must be checked.

front: Bloom filter size at 1% false positives?
back: About 9.6 bits per item and 7 hash functions: ~120 MB for 100 million IDs.
One key with so much traffic it saturates the single node it lives on. More nodes don't help.

front: Two fixes for a hot key?
back: A short-TTL local cache in each app server, or replicate the key under several names (key#0..key#N) on different nodes.
A large share of the cache disappears at once (synchronised expiry or an empty restart) and full load hits the database.
Add randomness to TTLs (e.g. 3,600 s ± 10%) so keys written together don't expire together.

front: Defences when the whole cache is cold?
back: Replicate across zones, warm before taking traffic, coalesce requests, and rate-limit or circuit-break database reads.
